title: Where is my partner? (Bava Metzia 84a)
hookLine: Resh Lakish, once a gladiator, becomes Rabbi Yochanan's study partner; after he dies, Yochanan can't be consoled
last: THE TALMUD KEEPS ITS HEROES' FLAWS, AND THEIR TURNING.

cards: A question about knives. When does a blade count as a finished tool: when it comes out of the furnace, or when it's plunged into water? It's a dry point of purity law, the kind the study house argued over.
Two old partners are arguing it. Rabbi Yochanan, the great teacher.
And Resh Lakish, the rough man from the riverbank whom Rabbi Yochanan drew into a life of study; another tractate says he had once sold himself to the arena.
On this ordinary question, one sentence is about to break them apart.

teach.b: Tractate Bava Metzia tells it. Rabbi Yochanan says the blade is finished when it leaves the furnace. Resh Lakish says when it's quenched in water.
And Rabbi Yochanan answers: a robber knows his trade. A jab at his partner's old life. Resh Lakish answers, stung: what good did you ever do me?
There, among the robbers, they called me master. Here, they call me master. Rabbi Yochanan replies: I brought you near, under the wings of the Divine Presence.
Both are wounded. The story says Resh Lakish fell ill. His wife, Rabbi Yochanan's own sister, came weeping and begged her brother to pray for him, for her children's sake.
He answered her with a verse from Jeremiah, about God caring for the orphan and the widow, and he did not relent. Resh Lakish died. And then the great teacher fell apart.
You may remember the next part: the sages sent him a brilliant student who only ever agreed with him, and it didn't help.

teach.h: WHERE ARE YOU, SON OF LAKISH?
teach.b: Rabbi Yochanan tore his clothes and wept, crying out: where are you, son of Lakish?
Where are you? The Talmud says he cried until his mind gave way, and the sages prayed for mercy for him, and he died. It's a hard page, and the tradition kept it whole.
It doesn't say who was right about the knives.
It says what a partner is worth: the person who argues with you until things come clear. And it measures that worth the hard way, by the empty chair.

how: In yeshivas and study programs, learners often study in pairs, and the story of Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish is told to show what a true study partner means.

games.q: what does “where is my partner?” mean?
o: a sage's search for a student who ran away
Rabbi Yochanan's cry for the partner he lost
a request to be paired with a new study partner

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.
p: finished when it leaves the furnace
where are you, son of Lakish?

s: the quarrel began over a question about blades
when a knife counts as finished: from the furnace, or from the water.
Rabbi Yochanan prayed for Resh Lakish when his sister begged him
he answered with a verse about God caring for orphans and widows, and did not relent.
a new student who always agreed comforted Rabbi Yochanan
it didn't help. he cried out: where are you, son of Lakish?

games.q: you're Rabbi Yochanan. your partner has just disagreed with you, sharply, about when a blade is finished. what do you say?
o: a fair point; let's work it through.
games.why: he takes a jab at his partner's old life. it costs them both everything, and the Talmud keeps the story whole.

practice: Bring to mind the person who pushes back on you and makes you clearer: a study partner, a spouse, a sibling, a friend who won't just agree. Remember one time they were right and you weren't.
Let gratitude come, if it comes, while the chair is still full.

wordCard.voice: Where is my partner? Rabbi Yochanan's cry for Resh Lakish, the partner who argued with him, after a quarrel neither of them could take back. Today's word.

orig.note: Resh Lakish: the name the Talmud uses for Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, Rabbi Yochanan's partner.
